threatManifold.title: 3D Riemannian Threat Manifold & Differential Calculus Variable Isolation
threatManifold.nonExpertHeadline: How 3D Geometry Separates Normal Population Growth from Real Voter Roll Anomalies
threatManifold.nonExpertAnalogy: Think of a healthy voter roll like a smooth, stretched rubber sheet (a 'manifold'). When a county grows naturally, its housing, mail forwardings, and polling places move together along that smooth sheet. By using calculus (partial derivatives) to hold two variables steady while measuring the third, we map every county into 3D space. Normal counties rest quietly on the sheet; true anomalies pull away from the sheet like mountain peaks.

equations.stateVector: r(c) = < X_domicile, Y_mobility, Z_velocity > in R^3
equations.partialIsolation: grad(Phi) = < dPhi/dX, dPhi/dY, dPhi/dZ > (Orthogonal Variable Isolation)

x.name: Spatial Domicile Compression (d_rho / dx)
x.description: Isolates single-family residences with 8+ voters (PB-01), dorms/apartments missing unit numbers (PB-02), and P.O. Boxes listed as physical homes (PB-04).

y.name: Identity & Interstate Drift (dS / dy)
y.description: Isolates Active voters receiving mail out-of-state (PB-03), suffix-disambiguated duplicate registrations (PB-06), and database migration typos (PB-05).

z.name: Temporal Surge & Precinct Strain (d^2V / dt^2)
z.description: Isolates mega-precincts exceeding 3,000–5,000 voters (PB-08), pre-election registration spikes (PB-07), and 25.9M voting history velocity.

correlations.pairLabel: Out-of-State Mail Forwardings (PB-03) vs. Intra-ZIP Duplicate Clusters (PB-06)
correlations.plainTitle: When Voters Move Without Updating Rolls, Duplicate Records Follow
correlations.rateOfChange: Every +10 Active out-of-state mail forwardings in a county corresponds to +4.2 intra-ZIP duplicate registration clusters.
correlations.commonManTakeaway: Counties with high residential turnover (college towns, military bases, and fast-growing suburbs) accumulate both out-of-state mail forwardings and duplicate registrations at the exact same time. Cleaning NCOA relocation backlogs automatically resolves nearly half of a county's duplicate footprint.

correlations.pairLabel: Total County Roll Volume vs. High-Density Residential Clusters (PB-01)
correlations.plainTitle: High-Density Clusters Scale with Urban & Campus Housing Concentration
correlations.rateOfChange: Each additional 10,000 registered voters adds an average of +8.7 high-density parcels (8+ voters at a single street address).
correlations.commonManTakeaway: Large counties naturally have more apartments, nursing homes, and dorms—which is why raw counts alone mislead people. By subtracting institutional and apartment buildings first, a Commissioner can see which counties actually have single-family houses with 10 to 25 legacy voters still on the roll.

correlations.pairLabel: Inactive Voter Roll Share vs. Single-Family High-Density Accumulation (PB-01)
correlations.plainTitle: Delayed Inactive-Roll Purges Directly Inflate 'Crowded House' Counts
correlations.rateOfChange: 30.4% of all voters sitting inside high-density addresses (7,076 of 24,905) are already marked Inactive—waiting on their 2-cycle NVRA removal clock.
correlations.commonManTakeaway: When someone sees '15 voters registered at one house,' it usually isn't 15 people living there today—it is three families who rented the house over 12 years and never cancelled their old registration. Separating Active from Inactive voters cuts the high-density alarm list by a third overnight.

correlations.pairLabel: Over-Capacity Mega-Precincts (>3,000 Voters, PB-08) vs. Active Out-of-State Drift (PB-03)
correlations.plainTitle: Fast-Growing Suburban Precincts Face Both Line Bottlenecks and Mail Drift
correlations.rateOfChange: Counties with 5+ mega-precincts (DeSoto, Harrison, Madison, Rankin, Hinds) account for 43.2% of all out-of-state active mailings statewide.
correlations.commonManTakeaway: Rapidly growing commuter counties experience a double squeeze: new subdivisions overload existing polling places past 5,000 voters while mobile families move across state lines. Splitting overloaded precincts and running NCOA address updates solves both bottlenecks together.

correlations.pairLabel: Manifold Axis X (Address Crowding) vs. Axis Y (Identity & Mail Drift)
correlations.plainTitle: Why 3D Variable Isolation Beats a Single Flat Score
correlations.rateOfChange: Partial derivative dZ_eq/dX = +0.34 and dZ_eq/dY = +0.29 along the smooth baseline surface; counties above Z_eq are true statistical outliers.
correlations.commonManTakeaway: Because address crowding (X) and mail drift (Y) only moderately overlap (r = 0.178), a single 1-to-100 score hides whether a county needs building-unit cleanup (like Oktibbeha/Lafayette) or polling-place splits (like DeSoto/Madison). Plotting X, Y, and Z in 3D lets every Election Commissioner see their county's exact maintenance recipe.

evangelismSteps.title: Separate Real Anomalies from Normal Buildings Before Anyone Panics
evangelismSteps.detail: Show your fellow Commissioners how Marigold automatically separates nursing homes, university dorms (PB-01/PB-02), and Jr./Sr. fathers and sons (PB-06) from true actionable items. That immediately builds trust with Circuit Clerks.

evangelismSteps.title: Isolate Your County's #1 Driver on the 3D Manifold
evangelismSteps.detail: Instead of arguing over raw totals, click your county on the 3D Manifold and toggle X (Addresses), Y (Relocations/Duplicates), and Z (Polling Place Strain). You will immediately see which single variable drives your county's workload.

evangelismSteps.title: Bring a 1-Page Peer Comparison to Your Next ECAM District Meeting
evangelismSteps.detail: Compare your county against similarly sized Mississippi peers using the 82-County Benchmark Table. When neighboring counties see that 98.7% of records pass cleanly and the remaining 1.3% can be fixed with standard NVRA postcards and 911 address tables, adoption becomes effortless.
